etymology: Hebrew meremoth, perhaps “heights” or “elevations,” the name of a priest, the son of Urijah the son of Koz, who repaired the wall of Jerusalem and weighed the vessels of the house of the LORD.
biblical_def: Meremoth was a priest, the son of Urijah the son of Koz, and a man of more than common diligence, for he is named twice among the builders of Jerusalem’s wall, repairing one portion of the breach and then a second piece over against his own house and beyond (Neh 3:4; Neh 3:21). Nor was the wall the whole of his service, for when Ezra came up from Babylon with the silver and the gold and the holy vessels of the house of God, it was into the hand of Meremoth that the treasure was weighed and delivered, that nothing be lost (Ezr 8:33). His name signifies “heights,” and his labour answered to it, for he was set to high and holy charges, both the keeping of the sanctuary’s gold and the raising of the broken wall. The dictionary honours that the people had a mind to work, every man over against his own house, and that Meremoth wrought a double portion when one had been enough. There is a pattern of faithfulness here, for the LORD is served best by those who do not measure their labour, but take up a second piece when the first is finished. Meremoth stands as a witness that the priest trusted with the holy things is the same who stoops to lay stone upon stone, and that all such honest toil, whether in the treasury or upon the wall, is reckoned by the great High Priest who will reward His faithful servants.
webster_summary: A priest, son of Urijah, who repaired two portions of the wall of Jerusalem and weighed the holy vessels brought up by Ezra.

etymology: Hebrew malkiyah, “the LORD is my King” or “my king is Jah,” a name borne by several men, here Malchijah the son of Rechab, ruler of part of Beth-haccerem, who repaired the dung gate of Jerusalem.
biblical_def: Malchijah the son of Rechab, the ruler of part of Beth-haccerem, is named among the builders of Jerusalem’s wall, and to him fell the repairing of the dung gate, which he built and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof (Neh 3:14). The name, which signifies “the LORD is my King,” is borne by several men of the return, among them a son of Harim and a goldsmith’s son who wrought upon the wall (Neh 3:11; Neh 3:31); but this Malchijah is marked by the meanest gate of all, the gate by which the refuse of the city was carried out to the valley. It was no honour in the eyes of men to be set over the dung gate, yet a ruler took the task and finished it with locks and bars complete. The dictionary honours that in the work of God the lowly office is not despised, for the people had a mind to work, every man over against his own portion, and no gate was beneath the dignity of a faithful builder. He whose name confessed the LORD as King was content to guard the humblest passage of the holy city. Malchijah stands as a witness that the King whom he named regards not the greatness of the task but the faithfulness of the worker, and that he who keeps the lowest gate of the city of God shall be owned by the King who Himself took the form of a servant.

etymology: Hebrew binnui, “building” or “a building,” a Levite, the son of Henadad, who repaired a portion of the wall of Jerusalem and sealed the covenant under Nehemiah.
biblical_def: Binnui the son of Henadad was a Levite who repaired another piece of the wall of Jerusalem, from over against the house of Azariah unto the turning of the wall, and even unto the corner (Neh 3:24). His name signifies “building,” a word singularly fitted to the man, for he was set to build, and his very name was a sermon upon his work. Nor did his service end when the wall was finished, for among those who sealed unto the sure covenant, setting their hands to the solemn engagement to walk in God’s law, the Levites are named, and Binnui among them (Neh 10:9). Thus he is found both raising the outward wall of the city and binding himself by oath to the inward law of the LORD, that the people might be a holy nation as well as a defended one. The dictionary honours that the same hands which laid the stones also signed the covenant, for the rebuilding of Jerusalem was no mere work of masonry but the renewing of a people unto God. There is a lesson here that walls without holiness are vain, and that the LORD would have His people both walled about and bound to His law. Binnui, the man whose name means building, stands as a witness that the LORD builds His house of living stones, and that the wall and the covenant alike point to that city whose builder and maker is God.

etymology: Hebrew bavvai, of uncertain meaning, perhaps “wishes” or “my goings,” a son of Henadad, ruler of the half part of Keilah, who repaired a portion of the wall of Jerusalem.
biblical_def: Bavai the son of Henadad, the ruler of the half part of Keilah, is named among the builders of Jerusalem’s wall, repairing the piece next after his brethren in the great labour under Nehemiah (Neh 3:18). He was of the house of Henadad, that Levitical family from which Binnui also came, so that brethren of one stock are found together upon the wall, each at his appointed portion. He was a ruler, set over half the district of Keilah, a town of the lowland of Judah where David of old had delivered the men of the city from the Philistines; yet this ruler did not count it beneath his station to take a trowel and labour at the stones. The meaning of his name is uncertain to us, and the Scripture records of him nothing but his lineage, his rule, and his work upon the wall; yet that is no small remembrance, for he is written among those who built when the city lay desolate and the enemy mocked. The dictionary honours that the people had a mind to work, rulers and ruled alike, every man over against his portion. Bavai stands as a witness that the providence of God set even the lesser-known rulers of Judah to a holy task, and that a man whose name we cannot certainly read is yet kept for ever in the record of those who built the wall of the city of God.

etymology: Hebrew meshullam, “recompensed” or “befriended, made whole,” a name borne by many men, here Meshullam the son of Berechiah, who repaired the wall of Jerusalem yet whose daughter married the son of Tobiah.
biblical_def: Meshullam the son of Berechiah, the son of Meshezabeel, repaired two portions of the wall of Jerusalem, one piece next unto Meremoth and another over against his own chamber (Neh 3:4; Neh 3:30). His name signifies “recompensed” or “made whole,” and his hands were diligent upon the work; yet the Scripture records of him a thing that should make every builder watch his own heart, for his daughter was given in marriage to the son of Tobiah the Ammonite, the bitter adversary who mocked the wall and conspired against the work (Neh 6:18). Thus a man who laboured to build the city by day was bound by marriage to the enemy who sought its ruin, and Tobiah had many in Judah sworn unto him because of these alliances. The dictionary marks this without flinching, for the LORD’s record is honest, and it warns that a man may put his hand to a holy work and yet entangle his house with the ungodly. There is a solemn lesson here against being unequally yoked, and against the friendship of the world that is enmity with God. Meshullam stands as a double witness: that the LORD remembers the labour of His servants’ hands, and that the same servants must guard their households from the snare of the adversary, lest the wall they build with one hand be undermined by the alliance they make with the other.

etymology: Hebrew chanun, “favoured” or “gracious,” here Hanun who with the inhabitants of Zanoah repaired the valley gate of Jerusalem, to be distinguished from Hanun king of the Ammonites.
biblical_def: Hanun is named among the builders of Jerusalem’s wall, for he with the inhabitants of Zanoah repaired the valley gate, built it, and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof, and a thousand cubits on the wall unto the dung gate (Neh 3:13); and a second Hanun, the sixth son of Zalaph, repaired another piece (Neh 3:30). His name signifies “favoured” or “gracious,” and he is carefully to be distinguished from Hanun king of the children of Ammon, who shamed the servants of David, cutting off their garments and their beards, and so brought war upon his people (2Sa 10:4). The one Hanun is a builder of the city of God; the other a despiser of the kindness of the LORD’s anointed, and the dictionary will not confound the gracious builder with the foolish king. This Hanun and the men of Zanoah took the valley gate, a great charge, and laboured a full thousand cubits of wall besides, a portion larger than many. The work was done not by one man but by a town gathered to the task, the inhabitants of Zanoah coming up to build the city that was not their own dwelling. Hanun stands as a witness that whole households and towns may give themselves to the LORD’s work, and that the favour his name confesses is shown most truly not in a king who scorns mercy but in humble men who build the walls of Zion together.

etymology: Hebrew shallum, “recompense” or “retribution, requital,” a name borne by many men, here Shallum the son of Col-hozeh, ruler of part of Mizpah, who repaired the fountain gate of Jerusalem.
biblical_def: Shallum the son of Col-hozeh, the ruler of part of Mizpah, repaired the fountain gate of Jerusalem; he built it, and covered it, and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof, and the wall of the pool of Siloah by the king’s garden, and unto the stairs that go down from the city of David (Neh 3:15). His name signifies “recompense,” and is borne by many in Scripture; but this Shallum is marked by the fountain gate and the pool of Siloah, the place of living waters that ran into the holy city. There is a sweetness in his portion, for of all the gates it was his to build the way unto the waters, by the king’s garden and the stairs of the city of David. The dictionary honours that this ruler covered the gate and finished it complete, sparing no part of the charge that fell to him. The pool of Siloah is the very water to which our Lord sent the man born blind, that he might wash and receive his sight, and Siloam is by interpretation, Sent. Shallum, who built the wall about those waters, stands as a witness that the LORD sets His servants to guard the places of His grace, and that the fountain gate of the earthly city points onward to Him who is the fountain of living waters, the Sent of the Father, to whom the thirsty are bidden come and drink.

etymology: Hebrew chanani, “gracious” or “the LORD is gracious,” here Hanani the brother of Nehemiah, who brought word of Jerusalem’s ruin and was afterward made a ruler over the city.
biblical_def: Hanani was the brother of Nehemiah, and it was he, with certain men of Judah, who came to Nehemiah in the palace at Shushan and brought the heavy tidings that the remnant in the province were in great affliction and reproach, the wall of Jerusalem broken down and the gates burned with fire (Neh 1:2). At this word Nehemiah sat down and wept, and mourned, and fasted, and prayed before the God of heaven, and out of his brother’s report came the whole great work of the rebuilding of the wall. Thus the labour began not with a sword nor a trowel but with a faithful brother who carried the truth, however grievous, to one who could be stirred to act. Afterward, when the wall was finished, Nehemiah gave Hanani charge over Jerusalem, with Hananiah the ruler of the palace, because he was a faithful man and feared God above many (Neh 7:2). His name signifies “the LORD is gracious,” and grace indeed it was that brought the news to the right ear and set a God-fearing man over the city. The dictionary honours that Hanani was trusted first to tell the truth and then to govern, and that the LORD reckons faithfulness and the fear of God above natural gifts. Hanani stands as a witness that great works of God often begin with one humble messenger who will not hide the ruin, and that the man found faithful in a small charge is set over a greater.
webster_summary: Hanani, brother of Nehemiah, who brought word of Jerusalem’s ruin and was made a ruler over the city.

etymology: Hebrew shechanyah, “dweller with the LORD” or “the LORD hath dwelt,” a name borne by several men, here Shecaniah the son of Jehiel who counselled the covenant, and Shecaniah the keeper of the east gate.
biblical_def: Shecaniah is a name borne by several men of the return, and two of them are joined to this season of repentance and rebuilding. The first is Shecaniah the son of Jehiel of the sons of Elam, who, when Ezra wept and confessed the great trespass of the people in taking strange wives, lifted up his voice and said, We have trespassed against our God, yet now there is hope in Israel concerning this thing; and he counselled a covenant to put away the strange wives, saying, Arise, for this matter belongeth unto thee; be of good courage, and do it (Ezr 10:2). The second is Shecaniah, keeper of the east gate, named in the rebuilding of the wall (Neh 3:29). His name signifies “dweller with the LORD,” and both men in their measure laboured that the LORD might dwell with a purified and a walled people. The dictionary honours that the one Shecaniah found the courage to name the sin and call for the hard covenant, and the other kept faithfully the gate appointed him. The work of God needs both the man who will rise and say, This belongeth unto thee, and the man who will quietly keep his gate. Shecaniah, whose name speaks of dwelling with God, stands as a witness that the LORD draws near to a people who put away their sin and keep their charge, and that the courage to begin a hard obedience is itself a gift of grace.

etymology: Hebrew berekyah, “the LORD blesseth” or “blessing of the LORD,” a name borne by several men, here Berechiah the father of Meshullam the builder, a Levite of the returned remnant.
biblical_def: Berechiah, the son of Meshezabeel, was the father of Meshullam who repaired two portions of the wall of Jerusalem, and through that son his name is twice written into the record of the rebuilding (Neh 3:4; Neh 3:30; Neh 6:18). A Berechiah is also named among the Levites who dwelt in the villages of the Netophathites and returned to keep the service of the house of the LORD (1Ch 9:16). His name signifies “the LORD blesseth,” a confession set in the very naming of his house, that the blessing of God is the portion of His people. Of Berechiah himself the Scripture records little beyond his fatherhood and his lineage, yet he is remembered chiefly as the father of a builder, one whose son took a trowel to the broken wall of the holy city. There is honour in this quieter kind of remembrance, for a man may serve the LORD’s cause through the children he begets and rears unto faithfulness. Yet the same record is honest, for the son of Berechiah, for all his labour, gave a daughter to the house of Tobiah the adversary; and so the father’s blessing must be sought afresh in every generation. Berechiah stands as a witness that the LORD blesses the line of His people, and that the godly father’s truest legacy is a seed that builds the walls of Zion and keeps itself unspotted from the friendship of the enemy.
